title: Trimurti, Avatars and Hindu Worship
welcome_lead: From the Trimurti to Krishna and Rama, explore the deities and devotional practices of Hindu life.
meta_desc: Religious Studies Adventure: Trimurti, avatars and Hindu worship.
final_note: You have entered the colourful world of Hindu devotion. Practice is as central as philosophy.

concepts.def: Threefold form of the divine: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer.
Incarnation of a deity, especially Vishnu, who is traditionally said to have ten avatars (dashavatara).
Devotional worship offered to deities at home and in temples, often using flowers, light and food.
Image or statue of a deity that becomes a focus of worship.
Festival of lights celebrated in autumn, marking Rama's return to Ayodhya and the victory of light.
Classical fourfold social order: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra — distinct from modern jati.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Trimurti highlights three cosmic functions. Vaishnavism centres on Vishnu and his avatars (especially Rama and Krishna); Shaivism on Shiva (often as Nataraja or as the lingam); Shaktism on the Goddess in forms like Durga and Kali. Despite apparent polytheism, most Hindus affirm an underlying unity.

Vishnu's traditional ten avatars (dashavatara) include Matsya (fish), Kurma (turtle), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha (in some traditions) and the future Kalki. Devotional traditions emphasise the lila — divine play — of Krishna especially.

Worship may take place at home shrines or in temples, with offerings of flowers, light, water and food. Major festivals include Diwali (lights), Holi (colours, spring), Navaratri/Durga Puja (Goddess), Janmashtami (Krishna's birth) and Mahashivaratri (Shiva). Pilgrimage to sites like Varanasi remains central.
